papers.title: Feedback-driven cardinality estimation for join queries
papers.one_line: corrects estimates from executed plans, no retraining

papers.problem: Independence assumptions make join estimates compound their error across the plan, and a retrained model is stale by the time it ships.
papers.idea: Treat the optimizer as a control loop: every executed plan already measures true cardinalities, so correct the estimator from that signal instead of learning the data distribution up front.
method: Logs actual row counts per plan node at execution time
Keys corrections by join-predicate signature, not by query text
Applies a multiplicative correction at estimation time; no retraining step
Falls back to the histogram estimate when a signature is unseen
contributions: generalizes corrections across queries touching the same joins
correction decays so stale signal cannot dominate
patch against PostgreSQL 17, scripts for JOB and CEB
results: vs the built-in estimator on CEB (Fig. 5)
strengths: Baselines were tuned, and the tuning is written down (Appendix B)
Correction needs no offline training set, so cold start is the current behaviour
Ablation separates the signature keying from the decay term
limitations: No result on update-heavy workloads; all benchmarks are read-only
[inference] our write rate may invalidate corrections faster than they decay
papers.for_us: Optimizer latency (P1): it replaces the histogram estimator we already isolate behind one interface, so a trial is a swap, not a rewrite.
takeaway: Closest thing to a drop-in win in this review.
One interface, public patch, tuned baselines.
notes: How it works: corrections are stored in a bounded LRU keyed by join signature; a decay factor halves a correction every N executions.
Baselines: PostgreSQL 17 with default and with tuned statistics targets; both reported.
Cost to try here: one week to port the patch, benchmark data already in the lake.
Relation to the other two papers in this theme: same signal, different placement.
